waypoints.title: Where Do Stars Come From?
waypoints.description: Every star you can see tonight was built out of a cloud of gas and dust. Our group at the University of Florida studies how that happens — especially for the rare, huge stars that are dozens of times heavier than the Sun. Those big stars light up galaxies, forge most of the chemical elements, and blow themselves apart as supernovae. This tour visits the places we have actually published on, and introduces the people who did the work. Press play, or step through with the arrows.
waypoints.image_caption: The Ginsburg group, University of Florida, May 2025.

waypoints.title: The Highway Into the Center
waypoints.description: The Milky Way is a barred spiral, and the bar acts like a set of on-ramps: gas from the disk runs inward along two narrow lanes and piles up in the Galactic Center. These 'dust lanes' are how the material for the next generation of Galactic Center stars gets delivered, and they are far less studied than the destination. Our group works on the clouds strung along them — including a newly found 60-parsec giant cloud sitting at the midpoint of the lanes, M4.7-0.8, nicknamed the Nexus and the Filament (Butterfield et al. 2025), and a set of twenty candidate bar clouds in which turbulent pressure heats the gas and appears to hold star formation back (Nilipour et al. 2024). The classic example of a cloud in this strange, high-speed population is Bania's Clump 2, known since the 1970s and lying along this same stretch of sky.

waypoints.title: Savannah Gramze: A Collision on the Ramp
waypoints.description: Gas coming down a bar lane sometimes overshoots the Galactic Center entirely and slams into the lane arriving from the other side. Graduate student Savannah Gramze found a site where that is happening: G5, a cloud out here at galactic coordinates l = +5.4, b = -0.4 (Gramze et al. 2023). Two gas components, one moving at about 50 and the other at about 150 kilometers per second, are connected by a bridge of material at intermediate speeds - the fingerprint of a collision in progress. The gas is around 60 degrees above absolute zero, warm for a molecular cloud, which is what a collision would do to it. Bania's Clump 2, the long-standing puzzle of a cloud with impossibly broad velocities, sits in this same region and is likely the same phenomenon.

waypoints.title: The Center of the Galaxy
waypoints.description: About 26,000 light years away sits the most crowded, most violent piece of our Galaxy: a ring of gas clouds called the Central Molecular Zone, wrapped around the Milky Way's central black hole. This picture combines radio light (from the MeerKAT telescope in South Africa) with infrared light (from the Spitzer Space Telescope). Image composite by Ashley Barnes. The gas here is denser, hotter, and more turbulent than anywhere nearby — a close-up model of the conditions in which most of the Universe's stars were made.

waypoints.title: ACES: Mapping the Whole Thing
waypoints.description: Our team led a large survey called ACES — the ALMA Central Molecular Zone Exploration Survey — using the ALMA observatory in Chile, 66 radio dishes on a high desert plateau, combined with the Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia. The result is the sharpest millimeter-wave picture of the Galactic Center ever made. Every bright knot is a clump of cold gas; some are building stars right now. Dozens of scientists worked on it, including most of the people you will meet in this tour.

waypoints.title: Molecules as Thermometers
waypoints.description: Radio telescopes do something cameras cannot: they identify molecules by the exact frequency of light those molecules emit, and they measure how fast the gas is moving. This map shows one molecule, isocyanic acid, glowing across the whole Galactic Center. Different molecules light up under different conditions, so a stack of maps like this works as a set of thermometers, pressure gauges, and speedometers laid over gas we will never visit.

waypoints.title: Finding the Shockwaves
waypoints.description: Switch to a different molecule — silicon monoxide — and the picture changes completely. This molecule is only released when dust grains are smashed apart, so it maps where gas is being violently slammed together: clouds colliding, jets from young stars, exploding stars. The bright streaks are the Galactic Center's crash sites. Comparing maps like these is how we tell gas that is merely dense from gas that is actually being disturbed.

waypoints.title: A Supernova Caught in the Act
waypoints.description: One of the first results out of ACES: a ring of gas about twenty light years across, whose shape and motion match a star that exploded inside a cloud and blew a bubble through it (Nonhebel et al. 2024). Explosions like this both destroy clouds and squeeze them. Which effect wins — whether a supernova shuts star formation down or sets off the next round — is one of the questions the survey was built to answer.

waypoints.title: Something We Cannot Explain
waypoints.description: This faint dot has gas moving at extraordinary speeds — hundreds of kilometers per second — but no matching bright star, no radio jet, no X-rays. We nicknamed it the MUBLO, for Millimeter Ultra-Broad-Line Object (Ginsburg et al. 2024). It might be a black hole of a mass we have never confirmed before, the wreckage of two stars merging, or a massive young star unlike any other. We still do not know. Surveys that map everything, rather than pointing at known targets, are how objects like this get found.

waypoints.title: The Brick: A Cloud That Won't Cooperate
waypoints.description: This cloud is nicknamed 'the Brick' because it is so dense and dark that it blots out the stars behind it. It holds enough material to make a hundred thousand Suns, yet it has produced almost no stars. By the usual rules it should be bursting with newborn stars. Figuring out what is holding it back tells us what actually controls star formation — which is why our group has spent years on this one object.

waypoints.title: Alyssa Bulatek: A Backwards Laser
waypoints.description: Graduate student Alyssa Bulatek studies the chemistry of the Brick, cataloging which molecules are present and what they reveal about the gas. One find: a particular methanol line in this cloud is a 'dasar' — the opposite of a laser (Bulatek et al. 2023). Instead of amplifying light, the gas absorbs it and appears as a shadow against the background. It is a rare state that only occurs under specific conditions, so it works as a diagnostic of the gas that produces it.

waypoints.title: Ice in the Dark
waypoints.description: With JWST we can find specific molecules frozen onto dust grains inside the Brick. These images are taken in narrow slices of infrared color, so ice reveals itself as a shadow at particular wavelengths, measured star by star through the cloud. We found frozen carbon monoxide almost everywhere in this cloud, and more of it than expected (Ginsburg et al. 2023), which changes how cold and how well-shielded we think the interior really is.

waypoints.title: The Colors of Ice
waypoints.description: That trick turned into a general method: measure the color of thousands of background stars and read off how much ice sits along each line of sight, without needing a spectrum for every star (Ginsburg et al. 2025). Savannah Gramze applied it far from the Galactic Center, mapping carbon monoxide ice across a star-forming filament in the Milky Way's 3-kiloparsec arm (Gramze et al. 2025). Ice is where the chemistry that eventually ends up in planets gets started.

waypoints.title: Sagittarius B2: The Big Factory
waypoints.description: If the Brick is a cloud that refuses to form stars, Sagittarius B2 is the opposite. It is the most massive cloud in the Galaxy and the most active nursery we know of, packed with newborn massive stars still buried in their birth material. This is a millimeter-wave view, so the glow is warm dust and gas rather than starlight. A single cloud like this one accounts for most of the star formation happening in the Galactic Center.

waypoints.title: Nazar Budaiev: Sgr B2 With JWST
waypoints.description: Graduate student Nazar Budaiev led the first JWST view of Sagittarius B2 (Budaiev et al. 2025). Infrared light escapes where the dust thins, revealing thousands of stars and glowing streamers of heated gas — and a surprise: star formation in this cloud is lopsided, with a sharp boundary between the active side and the quiet side. That is hard to explain with a gentle process; something appears to have squeezed the cloud from one direction.

waypoints.title: Counting the Newborn Stars
waypoints.description: Zoom into one knot of Sagittarius B2 and the picture is only a few light years across. Each compact blob is a young massive star, or a small group of them, still wrapped in the gas it is feeding on. Nazar Budaiev cataloged this population across the two densest clumps in the cloud (Budaiev et al. 2023), and separately mapped the water masers here — natural microwave beacons produced where jets from young stars slam into the surrounding gas (Budaiev et al. 2025).

waypoints.title: Desmond Jeff: Chemical Kitchens
waypoints.description: As a new massive star warms its cocoon, ices evaporate off the dust grains and the gas fills with complex molecules — alcohols, the chemical relatives of things in a kitchen. These regions are called hot cores. Desmond Jeff (PhD 2025) measured the temperatures of more than a dozen of them in the southern part of this cloud (Jeff et al. 2024). Undergraduate Mario Daley is cataloging the same region. Temperature matters: warmer gas resists breaking into small pieces, which may be why this environment favors making big stars.

waypoints.title: W51: A Star Factory Closer to Home
waypoints.description: Now we leave the Galactic Center for W51, about 17,000 light years away in the constellation Aquila — the most vigorously star-forming region in our part of the Galaxy, and close enough to study individual young stars in detail. It is one of 15 regions in ALMA-IMF, a large survey our group helps lead that asks whether the recipe for how many big versus small stars form is the same everywhere.

waypoints.title: Taehwa Yoo: How Clouds Break Apart
waypoints.description: Graduate student Taehwa Yoo studies how the dense clumps in W51 fragment into individual stars (Yoo et al. 2025). The finding: bigger clumps break into more pieces, but the mass stays concentrated in one dominant fragment. So a massive clump makes a massive star plus a handful of smaller companions — it does not simply split into many equal stars. That is the step that connects what we can see, gas clumps, to what we want to know, the stars they become.

waypoints.title: Two Telescopes, Two Different Answers
waypoints.description: Same patch of sky, different infrared colors. Each choice highlights something different: hot ionized gas, warm dust, shocked hydrogen, or the stars themselves shining through. It matters more than it sounds — in W51, only about one in ten young stars is seen by both JWST and ALMA. Each telescope catches a different stage of a star's infancy, so counting newborn stars with only one of them gives the wrong answer.

waypoints.title: The Undergraduates' W51
waypoints.description: W51 is also where several of our undergraduates work. Daelyn Sanders and Ethan Bhula are building a molecular inventory of the hot cores here — the list of chemicals present around each newborn massive star. Derod Deal works with Very Large Array radio data on ammonia masers, and Aden Dawson works on ground-based infrared imaging of the region from the Gran Telescopio Canarias. Undergraduate projects in this group produce catalogs and measurements that go into published papers.

waypoints.title: Orion: Salt Around a Young Star
waypoints.description: The Orion Nebula is the nearest place where massive stars are being born, about 1,300 light years away. Hidden behind this glow is Orion Source I, the closest massive protostar, with a disk of gas around it in which we detected ordinary table salt — sodium chloride — as a gas (Ginsburg et al. 2019). We have since found salt-bearing disks around several more massive young stars (Ginsburg et al. 2022). Salt is useful: its light comes from the innermost disk, so we can weigh the star at the center.

waypoints.title: Miriam Garcia Santa-Maria: The Chemistry
waypoints.description: Working out why salt appears in some disks and not others is chemistry, not just imaging. Postdoctoral researcher Miriam Garcia Santa-Maria works on the astrochemistry side of the group — salt, cosmic rays, and the reactions that run in Galactic Center gas. Molecules are the only thermometers and pressure gauges available inside a cloud we can never visit, so getting their chemistry right is what makes the measurements trustworthy.

waypoints.title: Theo Richardson: Simulating What We Should See
waypoints.description: Not all of the work involves telescopes. Theo Richardson builds models of young stars as they grow, then converts those models into fake observations — what a telescope would record if the model were true. Comparing fake to real is how we test whether a theory actually holds up, and it is the basis of a framework the group released for predicting the properties of young stellar populations (Peltonen et al. 2026). Theory and observation only work as a pair.

waypoints.title: The Big Question
waypoints.description: Underneath all of these pictures is one question: when a cloud collapses, what decides how many big stars and how many small stars come out? That recipe appears to be nearly the same everywhere we look, which is strange, because the clouds themselves are wildly different. Either something enforces the recipe, or we are being fooled by what we can and cannot see. Testing that is the through-line connecting every stop on this tour.

waypoints.title: The Group
waypoints.description: Undergraduates, graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and collaborators at observatories around the world. People here work on chemistry, on theory and simulations, on radio and infrared observations, and on the open-source software the whole field uses to handle datasets this size. The data behind these images is public, and so is most of the code that made them.

waypoints.title: Now It's Yours
waypoints.description: The tour is over, but the viewer is not. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, and use the menu button to jump back to any stop. Everything you have seen is real data from ALMA, JWST, MeerKAT, the Green Bank Telescope, and Gemini. More tours of these same regions — including a technical version of this one — are linked from the index page.
